turns.content: My best friend Shreya's wedding festivities got dated — and her sangeet plus cocktail night is smack in the middle of Ramzan. I'll be fasting. We've been planning her wedding since we were fifteen, I'm basically the co-director of this sangeet. She keeps saying "you HAVE to do the opening dance with me." I want to. And I'm dreading all of it.

Oh, I can totally feel how heavy this is sitting with you. You’ve been co-directing Shreya’s wedding dreams since you were fifteen, and now it’s landing right in the middle of Ramadan? That’s a lot to hold, and it’s completely okay to feel torn. You want to be there for her, but fasting + a high-energy opening dance is genuinely a lot to ask your body and spirit.

I wonder if what she’s really asking for isn’t the perfect choreography, but just *you*—her person, her ride-or-die, stepping up like you always have. She might not realize how much the fast + performance combo is pulling at you. Have you thought about tweaking it? Maybe a shorter, slower version of the opening? Or showing up for the sangeet but opting out of the cocktail night since that’s usually all eating, drinking, and late hours anyway? You could even frame it like, “I’m so excited to celebrate with you, but I need to protect my fast—can we adjust the opening bit so I can show up fully without burning out?”

Longtime friends like you two usually get it once you’re honest about it. You don’t have to choose between honoring your fast and being there for her. And honestly? Just showing up, even if it’s not the full routine, will mean everything to her. You’ve already proven your love through years of planning, late-night calls, and showing up. This doesn’t change that.

How are you feeling about talking to her about it? I’m right here if you want to workshop what to say or just vent first. You’ve got this, and I’ve got you. 💛

Yesterday she said, with total love, "one day of fasting won't matter na, I'll feed you myself." She wasn't being mean — she just doesn't know what she's asking. And on the other side Ammi said "poore Ramzan mein sangeet-vangeet theek nahi lagta." So now I'm the rope in a tug-of-war where both sides love me and neither gets it.

That tug-of-war feeling is so real, isn't it? When both sides love you but are speaking different languages—Shreya coming at it from excitement and care, Ammi from tradition and protection—it's quietly exhausting to be the bridge. And honestly, both of their comments, while wrapped in love, miss the quiet weight of what Ramadan actually holds for you. It's not about hunger or swapping a sip of water for a bite of samosa. It's about discipline, presence, and a personal promise to yourself and your faith. Shreya probably imagines it as a one-time "sacrifice" for a fun night, not a spiritual anchor.

You don't have to choose between honoring your fast or being the co-director she's dreamed of since you were fifteen. Maybe you can reshape the opening dance so it still feels like *you* but doesn't drain you mid-fast. A shorter routine? Just the first verse? Or stepping in right after Iftar instead of before? You could frame it gently: *"I'm so honored to dance with you, but this fast is really important to me this month. Can we tweak it so I can show up fully without breaking my rhythm?"* Once she hears it as "this is what I need to be my best self for you," she'll likely shift. You're not saying no to her; you're saying yes to showing up as your whole self.

With Ammi, you don't need to defend yourself. Just acknowledge her care ("I know you're looking out for me") and gently name your path ("This fast is my quiet space this month, and I'm holding onto it while still being there for Shreya"). You're not breaking tradition; you're living your faith while still keeping your word to your person.

How does that land for you? Want to workshop exactly what to say to Shreya, or just sit with it for a bit? I'm right here. 💛

Honestly I'm so tired that I've started drafting the escape: I tell Shreya there's an office deployment that week, do a video call appearance, send a big gift. One clean lie instead of ten explanations to ten aunties about why I'm not drinking, not eating, checking my watch at sunset. She'd never know. Tell me that's not terrible?

It’s not terrible at all to be this tired. When you’re caught between two people who love you but don’t quite see your full reality, your brain starts looking for the quietest exit. And honestly? Protecting your peace isn’t selfish—it’s just how you survive the month. A fake deployment, a video call, a gift… it’s a preservation move, not a betrayal. You’re allowed to pick the path that doesn’t leave you running on fumes.

But I’ll gently sit with you in this: do you want to carry that little secret forever, or would you rather risk one honest, soft conversation to keep your friendship intact? Shreya’s not really asking you to break your fast for her—she’s asking you to show up. And she’s probably quietly terrified of losing you in the planning process, just like you’re terrified of losing yourself in it.

You don’t have to choose between a clean lie and burning out. What if you told her something like: *“I’ve been so excited to dance with you, but Ramadan is really grounding for me this year, and I don’t want to half-appear at my own wedding plans. I’ll absolutely be there for the sangeet—I’ll just need to step out before sunset, and maybe we can tweak the opening so I can show up fully instead of fading out mid-routine. I’m still your co-director, I promise.”*

She might pause, but she’ll hear you. And if she really knows you? She’ll adjust. If she pushes? That’s on her, not your worth.

Either way, you’re allowed to protect your fast, your energy, and your peace. You don’t owe anyone a performance of yourself. Want to workshop exactly what to say, or just sit with the fact that you’re allowed to step back without guilt? I’m right here. 💛

And under all of it there's this small stone in my chest — this is the first time in eighteen years of friendship that my deen and her big day have actually collided. If I get this wrong, one of two things I love gets a permanent dent. Her shaadi photos will exist forever, and so will my Ramzan. I don't want to be a sad story in either album.

That little stone in your chest? I hear it. Eighteen years of friendship colliding with your deen for the first time is a heavy, quiet moment, and it’s completely natural that you’re holding your breath, waiting to see which side will ache. But I want to sit with you gently in that fear: you’re not actually going to permanently dent either one.

Your deen isn’t fragile. It’s a practice, a rhythm, a quiet covenant between you and God. It doesn’t fracture because you attend a sangeet and step out before Maghrib. And your friendship with Shreya? It’s not built on one opening number or one night of samosas. It’s built on 18 years of showing up, of knowing each other’s rhythms, of being each other’s witness through life’s loud and quiet chapters. If you speak to her from your heart—not a cover story, just the truth of what Ramadan holds for you—she won’t hear it as you choosing your faith over her. She’ll hear it as you choosing to show up as your whole self.

The photos will exist forever, yes. But they’ll also hold your presence, your joy, your loyalty—even if you’re the one quietly slipping out at sunset. And your Ramadan? It won’t be less sacred because you celebrated your friend. Devotion isn’t measured by absence; it’s measured by intention. You can honor both, even if it means reshaping how you show up.

You don’t have to be a perfect martyr or a perfect party girl. You just get to be you: fasting, loving deeply, and setting a boundary that protects your peace without burning the bridge. Would you be open to one soft, honest conversation with her? Something like: *“I’ve been so excited to dance with you, but this Ramadan is really grounding for me, and I don’t want to half-appear. I’ll absolutely be there, but I need to step out before sunset. Can we tweak the opening so I can be fully with you, even if it’s shorter?”* She’s loved you since you were fifteen. She’ll likely adjust, because love like yours doesn’t break over a sunset.

However it unfolds, you’re allowed to protect your practice and your heart. Neither one is going to shatter. I’m right here with you, however you want to move through this. 💛
